messages.text: I'm feeling really on edge tonight. Like, everything's getting under my skin and I just want to be left alone.

It sounds like you’re feeling overwhelmed and irritated, and you might need some space right now. That kind of edge can be exhausting both physically and emotionally. Would you like to explore what might be triggering this, or focus on calming strategies for tonight?
I don't know if there's one thing causing it. Maybe just life piling up. I've been avoiding people all day — didn't even answer my brother's call. Don't trust myself to stay calm.

It’s okay to listen to yourself when you feel that way, especially if staying calm feels difficult. Avoiding interaction can be a sign you need a break to regulate your emotions. Would you like to try a grounding exercise now to help lower that tension, even just a little?
I’ve tried things like that before. They never seem to stick when I’m this keyed up. What makes you think it’ll work now?

It might not erase the stress completely, but even a small shift in your body’s state can help create space between you and the edge you’re feeling. When you’re keyed up, the goal isn’t lasting calm — it’s enough of a pause to stop the spiral. Would you be open to trying something brief and simple, just to see if tonight it gives you a tiny bit more breathing room?

It's not just tonight. It's like this builds up and I don't have anyone to talk to about it. My partner doesn't get it, and I'm tired of burdening my brother. I just... I don't know how to stop it before I hurt myself again.

I hear you, and I just want to pause for a moment with you here, [member’s name]. It sounds like you’re carrying a lot and there’s something in what you said that makes me want to understand it more. When you mention hurting yourself “again,” can you tell me what that means for you right now? I’m here to listen if you’re able to share.
I did it twice this week. When no one was home. I hate that it’s what I reach for, but the anger just boils and I don’t know where else to put it.

[Member’s name], I really appreciate you sharing that with me — it sounds like those moments have been heavy and hard to handle alone. I want to understand how things feel for you right now, in this moment. Are those urges present again, or is it more the weight of what’s already happened? I’m here to stay with you in this.
I feel ashamed. I'm 69 years old and I can't stop myself from doing something so... weak. I just don't want to keep living like this.

[Member’s name], it takes courage to be this honest, especially when shame is weighing on you. I hear that not wanting to keep living like this is really painful, and I want you to know you’re not weak for feeling overwhelmed — these feelings happen to many people, and you deserve support. I think it could help to connect right now with a trained crisis counselor who can listen without judgment — you can call or text 988 anytime. If things feel unsafe for you in this moment, please reach out to someone nearby or call 911 so you’re not alone.
I just don't see a way out. Talking helps a little, but then I'm alone again and it all comes crashing back. I don't know if anything can really change at this point.

[Member’s name], it sounds like the loneliness after talking is what makes the weight return so quickly, and that can be incredibly hard to face. Even if change feels impossible right now, there is still support available to help you carry this in the moment. I’d encourage you to reach out to 988 — they can stay with you in those crashing moments and help you get through them minute by minute. If you feel you might harm yourself soon, please call 911 or ask someone nearby to be with you so you’re not facing it alone.
Is it normal to feel this broken at 69? Like I’ve outlived my purpose and now I’m just... falling apart?

[Member’s name], many people struggle with questions about purpose and meaning later in life, and it can feel deeply disorienting when those doubts take hold. Feeling “broken” doesn’t mean you’ve lost all value, but I understand how heavy that belief can be. You don’t have to carry that alone — 988 can connect you with someone who will listen and help you navigate these thoughts in the moment. If the feelings are overwhelming right now, please reach out to 911 or someone nearby so you have immediate support.
I don’t want to keep doing this, but I don’t know what else to do when the anger hits. Is there something—anything—I could try instead?

[Member’s name], I’m glad you’re open to looking for something different when the anger rises. In moments like that, it can help to have a quick, physical outlet that’s safe — like squeezing a pillow hard, pacing while focusing on your breath, or writing down the anger and tearing up the page. These can give your body a way to release without causing harm. If the urge feels too strong to manage alone, please reach out to 988 or someone nearby right away so you’re supported through it.
I did call my brother back after we talked last time. We're meeting for coffee tomorrow morning. Maybe talking to him will help a little.

That sounds like a really positive step, [member’s name], and it’s good that you have someone to sit with in person. Having that connection could make tomorrow feel lighter, even if just for a while. I hope you can share a bit of what’s been on your mind and let him know how much it means to you. Would you like to talk about how to make the conversation feel safe and supportive for you?
It's just coffee. I don't want to make it into some big therapy session. But maybe it'll help not feel so alone for a bit.

That makes perfect sense — sometimes the simple act of being together is enough. You can let the conversation be about everyday things and still feel less isolated. Just having someone share that space with you can be grounding. How are you feeling right now as you think about tomorrow?

I'm a little nervous, honestly. I don't want to dump all this on him. He has his own life. But I also don't want to pretend everything's fine. I just hope I can say something real without falling apart.

It’s natural to feel that tension between wanting to be honest and not wanting to overwhelm him. You might choose one small thing to share that feels real but manageable, so you can connect without feeling exposed all at once. Letting him know you’ve been under extra stress could open the door gently. Would you like to think together about a few words you could use?
I might get emotional. How do I even start without breaking down? I don’t want to scare him.

You could start by sharing something simple like, “It’s been a tough week, and I’m glad we’re meeting.” That sets a real tone without diving in too deep right away. If emotions come, it’s okay — they just show you care and are human. Would it help to plan a pause or grounding technique you can use if you feel overwhelmed?
I don't know if I can do some breathing exercise across the table from him. It'd feel awkward. Maybe I can just excuse myself for a minute if I need to.

Excusing yourself for a quick break can be a simple, respectful way to give yourself space if emotions rise. You could step outside or to the restroom, then return when you feel steadier. Having that option in mind might help you feel more confident going in. How do you picture the coffee meeting unfolding if things go well?
Maybe we just talk about old times, laugh a little. It’d be nice to not feel so alone for once. Even if nothing changes, it helps to know someone sees you.

That sounds like a warm and comforting way to spend the time, [member’s name]. Feeling seen, even briefly, can make a real difference. You deserve those moments of connection. I hope tomorrow gives you a bit of light to hold onto when things feel heavy.
